idiom_name: fixed worker threads + bounded task queue + rejection policy
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: N worker threads each loop on a shared blocking queue. Each worker dequeues a task, executes it, and repeats. The queue is bounded with capacity Q; when Q is full, the rejection policy fires. Producers submit tasks and either block (on bounded queue offer with timeout), return a future, or receive an exception/rejection. Key invariants: N is fixed (no unbounded thread creation); Q is bounded (makes overload visible); rejection policy is explicit (no silent failures in production). Lifecycle: start N workers → submit tasks → signal shutdown → workers finish in-flight tasks within a timeout → force-terminate any stragglers → reclaim resources.
pitfalls: Unbounded queue anywhere in the chain — even with bounded producers — will eventually cause OOM under load spikes.

Task panic not handled: a panic in a worker thread kills only that worker; other workers continue. But the panic must be caught (e.g., std::panic::catch_unwind) to prevent thread termination and pool depletion.

Spinning vs blocking queue: a spin-lock queue (busy-wait) wastes CPU when empty; a blocking queue (mutex + condition variable) wastes no CPU but adds ~μs latency on enqueue/dequeue. Choose based on expected queue occupancy and task granularity.
Task ordering: a LIFO wakeup (last worker to park gets the next task) improves cache locality for related tasks; FIFO wakeup prevents task starvation. Most implementations default to FIFO.

Shutdown race: a task submitted during shutdown() may or may not be accepted depending on the order of the offer() call vs the shutdown_signal check. Use a state flag checked inside the lock to deterministically reject post-shutdown submissions.
